01 / A FUNCTION RECOVERED

One missing call.
Four billion checks.

232possible float bit patterns

Dusklight stopped on an opaque string: cPGyc5FGjy0. The PlayStation 5 executable was asking for a math function that AnyPS5 didn’t yet provide. To get further, somebody had to find out exactly how that function behaved.

The contributor 0xRickx identified it as atanhf and read the compiled implementation bundled with another title. The disassembly pointed to FreeBSD’s math routines. In the author’s comparison, using the PC’s existing logarithm helper produced different result bits for 4.7% of inputs in the range [0, 1). The patch brought over the relevant paths instead. [1]

A mathematically plausible answer can still be the wrong answer for the program calling it. Floating-point rounding, error codes and exceptional values are part of the behavior being reconstructed. Those details survive compilation, even when the source that explained them is missing.

The author reported comparing the replacement with the bundled code across all 4,294,967,296 possible 32-bit input patterns, checking the returned bits, error state and floating-point exceptions. Collaborator adriadam10 then reported an exhaustive Linux comparison against the FreeBSD routines. [2]

LeandroLP23 tried the patch on two titles in Windows. With the prerequisite startup patch, Dusklight ran for 60 seconds. Wind Waker cleared the same missing-function error, then faulted elsewhere two seconds later. One piece of the system had become usable; the next failure was now visible. [3]

02 / MOVING THE PROGRAM

A console game.
A PC process.

AnyPS5 begins with a useful fact: the PS5’s CPU and the PCs it targets share the x86-64 instruction family. Much of the game’s compiled CPU code already speaks a language the host processor understands. The difficult work lies in the environment that code expects around it.

A game asks the operating system to load libraries, manage threads, open files and talk to graphics hardware. Its executable also has a format the operating system must know how to load. AnyPS5’s relinker changes that packaging and redirects the program’s imports to native replacements for the console’s system libraries. The intended result runs as an ordinary host process. [4]

Those imports use identifiers called NIDs. The mysterious string that stopped Dusklight is one of them: a label for a function the loader needs to find. AnyPS5 exposes replacements under the corresponding identifiers, allowing the operating system’s loader to connect the game’s request to an implementation. Bundled engine and middleware modules travel through the conversion too; the project’s contribution rules distinguish those from the system libraries it rebuilds.

→→→

Same CPU vocabulary. Different executable format, libraries, and operating-system expectations.

Sharing an instruction family does not make every instruction portable. The fixture at the top shows a real, narrow example from a checked-in test: six bytes encoding an AMD EXTRQ instruction become an Intel-compatible MOVQ plus padding. Switch the fixture and its 48 lamps display the actual bits before and after. Larger substitutions can require extra code and repaired control-flow references. [5]

The Intel conversion covers supported instructions already present in the executable and its modules. Instructions generated while a game runs are outside that pass. The repository also documents an Apple silicon route: emit an x86-64 Mach-O program with adjustments for Rosetta. That remains an x86-64 program passing through Rosetta’s translation. The boundaries matter when judging what “runs on another machine” actually means. [6]

Graphics add a second translation problem. The game’s shaders—small programs executed by the GPU—arrive as RDNA instructions. AnyPS5 decodes them, reconstructs their control flow and emits SPIR-V for Vulkan. A native CPU process still needs a graphics pipeline that understands the work it is submitting. Getting an import to resolve is one milestone on a much longer route to a correct frame. [7]

03 / MAKING THE WORK FINDABLE

The work has
an address.

The project’s own map turns this enormous undertaking into something a contributor can inspect. In the saved 13 October snapshot, it marks 3,197 of 3,615 declared library functions as implemented. Click the font library and a smaller frontier appears: 120 of 195 functions, with the unfinished names still attached.

That is also a way to organize a community. A developer can arrive at a particular library, investigate a particular call and submit a bounded change. A general implementation can then serve other titles that need the same behavior. The map gives thousands of separate investigations a common place to accumulate.

A map of declared functions.Pick a library, or inspect a tile.

The map tracks declarations known to the project. Its implemented count can include inert stubs; it is not a game-compatibility score. Original diagram by AnyPS5. How progress is counted ↗

04 / THE PUBLIC WORKSHOP

Who keeps
building?

315 accounts landed a pull request.
195 came back for another.

The GitHub repository was created on 3 August. By the 13 October snapshot it had 33,740 stars, 2,916 forks and 2,518 merged pull requests. Of 6,802 commits in the captured history, 4,622 carry author dates in the seven days from 6–12 October. The activity is concentrated, and the work is distributed: 315 distinct accounts authored merged pull requests, 195 of them more than one. [8]

GitHub cannot tell us what drew each contributor here or what caused the attention. It does show what happened after people arrived: patches were accepted, and many authors had further work merged. The practical question is how hundreds of contributors can work on parts of the same enormous problem.

The contribution guide supplies part of the machinery for working at this scale. Changes must address general behavior rather than a workaround for one title. An unimplemented path should fail visibly. An assumption that cannot yet be verified goes into technical debt. Contributors are asked to check for overlapping work and keep each pull request to one topic. [9]

That discipline makes the atanhf thread legible. A reader can trace the failure, the proposed behavior, the test and the remaining assumption about the system library. Another contributor can challenge a detail or try another title without reconstructing the entire investigation. Public review turns an individual discovery into knowledge the next patch can use.

AI assistance is already inside that process. The atanhf PR declares it; the commit credits Claude Opus as a co-author. The later Windows test report also declares Claude Code assistance. The record establishes participation, while leaving the division of labor between person and model largely unspecified. [10]

Recovering behavior from compiled code gives a coding agent a demanding assignment. The replacement has to agree with a program that already exists, down to details a human might never notice during a short play session. The human author remains responsible for the contribution under the project’s rules. The test cases, comparison reports and review comments give everyone else something firmer to judge than confidence in a generated answer.

THE COMPILED FRONTIER

What survives
the source.

A binary has lost much of what makes source code comfortable: names, comments, abstractions, the explanation of why a branch exists. It retains instructions, interfaces and behavior. AnyPS5’s contributors work outward from those surviving facts, replacing the surrounding pieces until a program built for one environment can function in another.

The atanhf patch contains the larger story in miniature. An opaque identifier became a recognizable function. Disassembly led back to public math routines. A proposed replacement met billions of comparisons. Other contributors checked it, and the next failure became a new problem somebody could investigate.

That is the standard worth carrying into agent-assisted engineering: make the path from observation to implementation to evidence available for inspection. A model can help expand the search; a public test and review process can make the result useful to strangers.

The headline is an engineering provocation. Software licenses still govern reuse, and a compiled program does not come with its original author’s explanation. Yet the work here shows how much can be recovered, tested and shared. The executable can be the beginning of an engineering project.
